synopsis: The booklet recommends disciplined expert review and adversarial challenge so a heavy off-road validation plan can withstand scrutiny of fog, low contrast and operation at the edge of its envelope; the red team's task is to attack whether the safety claim can be supported by the deadline, not proofread the plan [f9395, f9961, f16358]. Its proposed sequence is 8–12 interviews in months 1–2, elicitation in month 2, a pre-mortem in month 3, an independent red team in month 4 and a gate review with recorded dissent in months 5–6; it also recommends a second pre-mortem before delivery readiness [f16367, f9666]. Pre-mortems draw on 1989 prospective-hindsight experiments, and the one direct test found involved 178 students in 2010 and reduced confidence more than four alternatives, but evidence of improved real engineering-programme outcomes was not found [f9660, f9661, f9662, f9664]. Across 33 structured-elicitation applications, fewer than one third of experts met the statistical-accuracy criterion, so numerical judgments should be calibrated where practical and otherwise expressed as ranges with disagreement preserved; Delphi consensus does not establish correctness [f9488, f9952, f9953, f16366]. Review evidence favors seeking genuine skeptics and identifying rejection-critical weaknesses, but controlled evidence that red teams improve engineering outcomes—and causal evidence for these planning methods in safety-critical virtual validation—was not found [f16361, f9845, f9848, f9964, f10298].
